pos: n. (Janos Sylvester, c. 1504–1552, translator of the first printed Hungarian New Testament)
etymology: Hungarian Janos from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Latin Sylvester, of the woods, a humanist latinisation of Erdosi.
biblical_def: Janos Sylvester studied at Krakow and then at Wittenberg, where he heard Luther and Melanchthon, and came home to Hungary to do for his own language what Luther had done for German. At the press that Tamas Nadasdy maintained at Ujsziget near Sarvar he produced in 1541 the first printed Hungarian New Testament, translated from the Greek rather than from the Vulgate, with marginal notes and a verse preface in Hungarian classical metre. He had already written the first Hungarian grammar. The dictionary names him at the head of this batch because the Reformation in Hungary begins, as everywhere, with a translated text: the year his New Testament appeared is the year the Turks took Buda, and the kingdom that had printed it ceased in that generation to exist as one country. The book outlasted the kingdom. Three centuries of Hungarian Protestantism — under Ottoman occupation in the middle, Habsburg Counter-Reformation in the west, and a Reformed principality in the east — rested on the fact that the New Testament could be read in Hungarian before any of those settlements was fixed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines version as a translation, and grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety.
webster_full: VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
GRAM'MAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.
VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.

corruption_summary: He printed the first Hungarian New Testament from the Greek in 1541, the year the Turks took Buda.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a nation's Bible follows its political security — that translation is the fruit of settled times. Hungary's was printed into a collapse. Within months of the New Testament leaving the press the central third of the kingdom was under Ottoman rule and the rest divided, and the book went on being read in all three fragments.

The principle to recover is that the word of God is not underwritten by the state that happens to shelter it, and that it keeps working when the state does not. “And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8) is the Pentecost question Hungary could answer from 1541 onward. The alternative is Paul's warning: “for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). And the promise does not depend on the kingdom: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).

pos: n. (Matthias Devai Biro, c. 1500–1545, the first Hungarian reformer, called the Hungarian Luther)
etymology: Hebrew Mattithyah through Greek Matthias, gift of the LORD; Hungarian Biro, a judge.
biblical_def: Matthias Devai Biro went to Wittenberg in 1529, lodged in Luther's house, and came back to preach justification by faith in Hungarian towns that had never heard it. He was arrested, examined at Vienna and imprisoned, released, and spent the rest of a short life moving from patron to patron ahead of the authorities. He wrote the first Hungarian orthography and a catechism-like exposition of the Ten Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer in Hungarian, and in his later years he came to hold the Supper as the Reformed churches held it, which cost him Lutheran friends and earned him the name of sacramentarian. The dictionary records that movement without embarrassment: Devai followed the text where it led, from Wittenberg toward Zurich, and the Hungarian church followed him. He died before any of the settlements that would divide his countrymen were in place, having done the one thing a first reformer can do, which is to put the gospel into the language and let others build.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines justification as remission of sin and absolution from guilt, and sacramentarian as one who holds a figurative presence in the Supper.
webster_full: JUSTIFICA'TION, n. In theology, remission of sin and absolution from guilt and punishment; the act of acquitting.
SACRAMENTA'RIAN, n. One who holds that the bread and wine are signs and seals, not the natural body and blood.
ORTHOG'RAPHY, n. The art of writing words with the proper letters according to common usage.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.

corruption_summary: Luther's Hungarian lodger, imprisoned for preaching justification, who ended holding the Supper as Zurich did.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of a man's change of mind as either betrayal or growth, according to taste, with no attention to whether the change was made under the text. Devai moved on the Supper because he was persuaded from Scripture, and he paid for it in friendships at Wittenberg.

The principle to recover is that the Supper is a communion and a showing forth, and that the elements are signs and seals which the Spirit uses, not the natural flesh of Christ handled by a priest. “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63). Paul's own term is participation, not transmutation: “The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” (1Co 10:16). And the ground of all of it is the article he was imprisoned for: “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28).

pos: n. (Imre Ozorai, fl. 1535, author of the first Hungarian Protestant book)
etymology: Hungarian Imre, a form of Germanic Emmerich, whole-ruler; Ozorai, of Ozora, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Imre Ozorai studied at Wittenberg and Krakow and in 1535 published at Krakow the book usually reckoned the first Protestant work printed in Hungarian, an argument on Christ and His church against the Roman claims. Almost nothing else of his life is recorded; he preached in the Bekes region and then disappears from the sources. The dictionary gives him an entry for the book, and for what the book is: an argument about the church addressed to Hungarians in Hungarian at a moment when the kingdom's own bishops were mostly either dead at Mohacs or scrambling for political footing. Ozorai's thesis was that the church is where Christ's word is, not where a hierarchy says it is, and that the marks of a true church are therefore findable by a layman with a Bible. That claim is the hinge of the whole Reformation, and it reached the Hungarian plain in print six years before the New Testament did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines church as the collective body of Christians, and mark as a token or evidence by which a thing is known.
webster_full: CHURCH, n. The collective body of Christians, or of those who profess to believe in Christ and acknowledge him to be the Saviour of mankind.
MARK, n. A visible sign or impression; a token or evidence by which a thing may be known.
HI'ERARCHY, n. An ecclesiastical establishment with authority graduated by ranks.
TRACT, n. A written discourse or dissertation of no great extent; a small pamphlet.

corruption_summary: His 1535 Krakow book, the first Protestant work in Hungarian, argued that the church is where Christ's word is.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the identification of the church with its institutional continuity, so that the question of which body is the true church gets settled by succession lists rather than by the marks Scripture gives. Ozorai wrote for readers whose bishops had largely vanished and who needed to know whether they still had a church at all.

The principle to recover is that Christ constitutes His church by His word and presence, and that His sheep can identify His voice. “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20). The flock knows its own shepherd: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (Joh 10:27). And the foundation named is apostolic doctrine with Christ Himself as cornerstone — “Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20).

pos: n. (Martin Kalmancsehi Santa, c. 1500–1557, called the Hungarian Zwingli, superintendent at Debrecen)
etymology: Latin Martinus, of Mars, warlike; Kalmancsehi, of Kalmancsa, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Martin Kalmancsehi Santa had been a canon of Gyulafehervar before the gospel reached him, and he spent the rest of his life carrying the Reformed doctrine of the Lord's Supper eastward across Hungary against Lutheran resistance. He preached at Mezotur, Debrecen, Munkacs and Beregszasz, was repeatedly driven out, stripped altars and images where he was given leave, and died as the first Reformed superintendent of the Debrecen district — the see that made the eastern Hungarian church Calvinist rather than Lutheran for the next four hundred years. The dictionary honours the stripping of the altars as well as the preaching. Kalmancsehi held that the Supper is a communion in the body of Christ received by faith, not a bodily presence to be adored on a table, and that what cannot be adored ought not to be dressed as if it could. The Hungarian Reformed Church dates its sacramental settlement from him and from the synods that followed him at Debrecen.

SUPERINTEND'ENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of some place, person or business.

corruption_summary: He carried the Reformed doctrine of the Supper across eastern Hungary and stripped the altars where he could.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the reduction of iconoclasm to vandalism, as though the Reformers who cleared churches were acting out a temperament. Kalmancsehi was acting on the second commandment and on a doctrine of the Supper: if Christ's body is in heaven and received by faith, then an altar furnished for adoration teaches the congregation a lie every week it stands.

The principle to recover is that God names the manner of His own worship and refuses His glory to images. “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4). The refusal is His own, not the Reformer's: “my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8). And the Supper is given as a proclamation of a death, not a presence to be gazed at — “ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26).

pos: n. (Mihaly Sztarai, c. 1500–1575, preacher and hymnwriter of the Hungarian south under Ottoman rule)
etymology: Hungarian Mihaly from Hebrew Mikael, who is like God; Sztarai, of Sztara, a place-name surname.
biblical_def: Mihaly Sztarai was a Franciscan who had studied at Padua, fought or at least served at Mohacs, and came out of the catastrophe a Protestant preacher. For some twenty years he worked the Baranya and Tolna country of southern Hungary, which was under direct Ottoman administration and therefore outside the reach of both Habsburg bishops and Habsburg armies; by his own account he and his colleague planted something like a hundred and twenty congregations there. He wrote hymns that ordinary villagers could sing and two dramatic dialogues mocking the priesthood he had left. The dictionary keeps him as the clearest case of a gospel advance that owed nothing to a Christian magistrate. The Turk taxed the villages and did not much care what they believed; into that indifference the word went, carried by two men on foot with a hymnbook. It is a standing rebuke to the assumption that the church needs favourable conditions, and a standing warning against mistaking political protection for the Spirit's work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hymn as a song or ode in honour of God, and itinerant as wandering, not settled, passing from place to place.
webster_full: HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God, and among pagans, in honour of some deity.

TRIB'UTE, n. An annual or stated sum of money or other valuable thing, paid by one prince or nation to another.

corruption_summary: Under Ottoman rule he and a colleague planted some hundred and twenty congregations in southern Hungary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the quiet confidence that the church grows where she is favoured and shrinks where she is not, which makes political access look like a means of grace. Sztarai's field had no Protestant prince, no endowment and no protection; it had a Muslim tax collector and a road.

The principle to recover is that the increase is God's and the means are His appointed ones. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). The door is opened by Christ and cannot be closed by an empire: “behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength” (Rev 3:8). And the planter is not the giver — “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6).

pos: n. (Gal Huszar, c. 1512–1575, itinerant printer-preacher and editor of the first Hungarian hymnbook)
etymology: Hungarian Gal, a form of Latin Gallus; Huszar, a light horseman, from the Hungarian cavalry term.
biblical_def: Gal Huszar carried a press. Driven out of Magyarovar, Kassa, Debrecen and Komjati in turn, he moved his types with him and printed wherever a patron would shelter him, issuing Hungarian hymns, postils and polemic from four or five towns across thirty years. His collection of 1574, building on an earlier gathering of 1560, is the first substantial Hungarian Protestant hymnbook, and the tunes and texts in it were still being sung in Reformed villages centuries later. He was also a preacher and for a time superintendent, and he was imprisoned at least once. The dictionary names him as the type of a trade the Reformation invented: the pastor-printer, who understood that a sermon reaches a village and a printed hymn reaches a county. Hungary was too divided for any central Protestant authority to hold, and the thing that held instead was a repertoire of Hungarian psalms and hymns in print, which any congregation could buy and no occupying power bothered to suppress.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines printing as the art of impressing letters on paper, and hymnbook as a collection of hymns for public worship.
webster_full: PRINT'ING, n. The art or practice of impressing letters, characters or figures on paper, cloth or other material.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honour of God; a sacred song.

corruption_summary: A hunted printer-preacher whose 1574 collection is the first great Hungarian Protestant hymnbook.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the separation of the ministry of the word from the labour of producing and distributing it — as if preaching were spiritual and publishing merely commercial. Huszar did both with the same hands and in the same danger, and the press he dragged between towns did more lasting work than the pulpits he was thrown out of.

The principle to recover is that God commands His word to be written plainly and put where it can be carried. “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). When Jehoiakim burned the roll the answer was another roll: “Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words” (Jer 36:28). And the company that publishes is itself the Lord's doing — “The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11).

pos: n. (Stephen Szegedi Kis, 1505–1572, Hungarian Reformed theologian and pastor, prisoner of the Turks)
etymology: Greek Stephanos, a crown; Hungarian Szegedi, of Szeged; Kis, little, small.
biblical_def: Stephen Szegedi Kis studied at Wittenberg, taught and pastored through the Ottoman-held middle of Hungary, and served for many years at Rackeve on the Danube. In 1561 the Turks seized him, held him some two years, and his congregation and friends bought him back. Out of a working ministry conducted under occupation he produced two substantial Latin books: a systematic theology arranged as commonplaces, which was printed at Basel and read across Reformed Europe, and a long polemic against the Roman pontiffs. The dictionary records the oddity deliberately. A pastor in a Turkish-administered market town, who had been a prisoner in a Turkish gaol, wrote a dogmatics that Swiss and German divines bought and cited. Hungary was not a periphery receiving Reformed theology; it was a place where Reformed theology was written, under conditions that would have excused a man from writing anything at all.

THEOL'OGY, n. Divinity; the science of God and divine things.

corruption_summary: A pastor under Ottoman rule, two years a Turkish prisoner, who wrote a dogmatics printed at Basel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the geography of condescension, in which serious theology is produced at the centre and received at the edges. Szegedi Kis wrote at the edge, in a town paying tribute to Constantinople, and the centre bought his book.

The principle to recover is that God is not hindered by the circumstances of His servants, and that bonds do not bind the word. “I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). Paul found that the imprisonment itself served the gospel: “the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Phi 1:12). And the church is told to feel her prisoners as her own body — “Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them” (Heb 13:3).

pos: n. (Peter Bornemisza, 1535–1584, Hungarian Lutheran preacher, printer and author of postils)
etymology: Greek Petros, a stone; Hungarian Bornemisza, literally one who drinks no wine, a nickname surname.
biblical_def: Peter Bornemisza studied at Padua, Wittenberg and Vienna, preached at Semptem and Detrekö, served as a Lutheran superintendent, and ran his own press. His chief work is a vast set of Hungarian postils — sermon expositions on the gospel readings, printed in five folio volumes so that preachers in poor parishes without libraries had something sound to work from, and householders had something to read on a Sunday evening. He also wrote a Hungarian version of the Electra story and a remarkable catalogue of the temptations he had observed in his own congregations. The dictionary values the postils above the drama. Bornemisza understood that a Reformation stands or falls on whether the second-rate preacher in the back country has access to sound exposition, and he spent his own money and press on supplying it. The humility of that calculation — writing for the man who cannot write — is itself a pastoral act.

Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a contempt for the aids a preacher uses, as though originality were the measure of faithfulness and borrowed exposition a species of fraud. Bornemisza wrote for men with no books, in parishes with no money, and the result was that their congregations heard the text opened instead of a guess.

The principle to recover is that the aim of preaching is understanding, and that whatever serves understanding is legitimate. “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). Paul's plan for continuity is deliberately reproductive: commit it “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). And the priest's mouth is the place the people are to find knowledge — “the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7).

pos: n. (Gaspar Heltai, c. 1510–1574, printer and preacher at Kolozsvar, Bible translator and chronicler)
etymology: Hungarian Gaspar, from the traditional name of one of the eastern magi; Heltai, of Heltau, a Transylvanian Saxon place-name.
biblical_def: Gaspar Heltai was a Transylvanian Saxon who learned Hungarian as an adult and then spent his life printing in it. From his press at Kolozsvar came a large part of the Old Testament in Hungarian, a Hungarian chronicle of the kingdom, a dialogue on drunkenness, fables, and a stream of theological books. He began as a Lutheran, moved with his city to the Reformed position, and in his last years went further, into the antitrinitarian camp that Transylvania's unusual toleration had allowed to organise under Ferenc David. The dictionary states that plainly rather than passing over it. Heltai's presswork served the Hungarian Bible and the Hungarian language permanently; his final doctrinal position denied the Godhead of the Son and was error. Transylvania is the one place in sixteenth-century Europe where Reformed, Lutheran, Roman and antitrinitarian churches were all tolerated by law, and the lesson the dictionary draws is not that toleration is wicked but that a church which has no confession to hold men to will lose some of her best workmen to heresy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Arian as one who denies the divinity of Jesus Christ, and toleration as the allowance of religious opinions by law.
webster_full: A'RIAN, n. One who adheres to the doctrines of Arius, who denied that Jesus Christ was consubstantial with the Father.
TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of that which is not wholly approved; the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
PRINT'ER, n. One that prints books, pamphlets or papers.
CHRON'ICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
scriptures: Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Tit 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;
Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father: (but) he that acknowledgeth the Son hath the Father also.
corruption_summary: His press served the Hungarian Bible; his last years went over to the Transylvanian denial of Christ's Godhead.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to name is antitrinitarianism — the position advanced in Transylvania by Ferenc David and the Italian physician Giorgio Biandrata, and refined in Poland by Faustus Socinus, that the Son is a creature and not God of God. The Diet of Torda allowed it a legal standing no other European state gave it, and Heltai, the printer who had done more than almost anyone for the Hungarian Scriptures, finished among its adherents. The dictionary names the drift because the men who drift are rarely the careless; they are often the industrious, who have been given a great deal of work and never required to subscribe a confession.

The answer is the opening of John's Gospel, which the Hungarian Bible Heltai printed contains: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1). Thomas addressed the risen Christ as “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28) and was not corrected. Paul calls Him “the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ” (Tit 2:13). And John draws the consequence for anyone who separates the Son from the Father: “Whosoever denieth the Son, the same hath not the Father” (1Jo 2:23).

pos: n. (Albert Szenci Molnar, 1574–1634, Hungarian psalmist, lexicographer and translator of the Heidelberg Catechism and the Institutes)
biblical_def: Albert Szenci Molnar spent most of his adult life in Germany — Wittenberg, Heidelberg, Herborn, Marburg, Oppenheim — working for a church he could seldom live among. He made a Latin-Hungarian dictionary and a Hungarian grammar that held the field for two centuries; he revised and reprinted the Karoli Bible twice, at Hanau in 1608 and Oppenheim in 1612, in smaller formats that a household could afford; he translated the Heidelberg Catechism and Calvin's Institutes into Hungarian; and in 1607 he put the whole Genevan Psalter into Hungarian verse, keeping the Genevan tunes. That Psalter is the one indispensable item on the list. Hungarian Reformed people have sung Molnar's psalms continuously from 1607 to the present, through Habsburg repression, the galley-slave years of the persecuted ministers, and two world wars. The dictionary names him as the man who gave a scattered and frequently illegal church a book she could carry in her mouth, which is the one possession no edict can confiscate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines psalter as the Book of Psalms, and lexicon as a dictionary or vocabulary of a language.
webster_full: PSAL'TER, n. The Book of Psalms; often applied to a psalm-book, or a book containing the psalms separately printed.
LEX'ICON, n. A dictionary; a vocabulary or book containing an alphabetical arrangement of the words in a language.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
INSTITU'TION, n. A system of elements or rules; that which is appointed or established.
scriptures: Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
Now therefore write ye this song for you, and teach it the children of Israel: put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the children of Israel.
Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage.
corruption_summary: His 1607 Hungarian Psalter has been sung continuously ever since, through every persecution the church met.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern churning of congregational song, in which a repertoire lasts a decade and nothing is learned by heart. Molnar's psalms were learned by heart, which is why they survived a century in which Hungarian Reformed ministers were sent to the Mediterranean galleys and their churches taken away.

The principle to recover is that God puts His word into His people's mouths in song precisely so that it will survive what their institutions do not. Moses was commanded to write a song and teach it to Israel: “Now therefore write ye this song for you, and teach it the children of Israel: put it in their mouths” (Deu 31:19). The exile's question is answered by singing anyway — “How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4) — and the pilgrim's testimony is that the statutes themselves became the songs: “Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psa 119:54).

“Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage” (Psa 119:54) — sung through the galley-slave years.
“How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4) — a life spent working in Germany for Hungary.
